messages.subject_clean: SEM using correlation matrix in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves,

Thank you very much for your helpful response and for explaining the use of likelihood = "wishart". I also greatly appreciate the improvements you made in the new version(0.7.2.3257) of lavaan. With the new version of lavaan and the following code, we were able to reproduce the results reported in Table 4 of Cudeck (1989) exactly:

mod_5 = '
     #loadings of MVs on LVs
      f1 =~ L01*fr + L02*en + L03*hi
      f2 =~ L04*ar + L05*al + L06*ge

     #unique variances
     # these theta estimates have been deleted
     #factor variances and covariances
      f1 ~~ 1*f1           # fix LV variance at 1.0
      f2 ~~   f1 + 1*f2
      '
m5fit = lavaan(model = mod_5, meanstructure = FALSE,
               std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, auto.fix.first = FALSE,
               sample.cov = cor1, sample.nobs = 220,
               likelihood = 'wishart',
               estimator  = 'ML',
               correlation = TRUE)

The parameter estimates, standard errors, and ML chi-square now match the corresponding results reported by Cudeck. However, we have encountered one remaining issue. lavaan provides the point estimates of the unique variances, but it does not appear to provide their standard errors. The standard errors of the unique variances are reported in Table 4 of Cudeck's article. I would be very grateful if you could help me understand why lavaan does not produce the standard errors for the unique variances and whether there is a way to obtain them.
Best,
Asghar

messages.subject_clean: SEM using correlation matrix in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> lavaan provides the point estimates of
> the unique variances, but it does not appear to provide their standard
> errors. The standard errors of the unique variances are reported in
> Table 4 of Cudeck's article.

The unique variances are no longer free parameters. They are a
(deterministic) function of the other parameters. In principle, one
could use the delta rule to compute standard errors for these 'defined'
parameters (as we do with the := operator), but lavaan does not do that
out of the box.

So if you really want them, you need to define them explicitly using the
:= operator. In this case, they are easy. The model-implied variance per
item is just lambda squared, as the variance of the latent variable is
fixed to one, so we have:

model <- '

      #loadings of MVs on LVs
       f1 =~ L01*fr + L02*en + L03*hi
       f2 =~ L04*ar + L05*al + L06*ge

      #factor variances and covariances
       f1 ~~ 1*f1

       f2 ~~ 1*f2
       f2 ~~ f1

       resvar.fr <http://resvar.fr> := 1 - L01^2
       resvar.en := 1 - L02^2
       resvar.hi := 1 - L03^2
       resvar.ar <http://resvar.ar> := 1 - L04^2
       resvar.al <http://resvar.al> := 1 - L05^2
       resvar.ge <http://resvar.ge> := 1 - L06^2
'

fit = lavaan(model = model, correlation = TRUE, likelihood = "wishart",
              sample.cov = cor1, sample.nobs = 220)

resulting in:

lavaan 0.7-2.3265 ended normally after 19 iterations

   Estimator                                         ML
   Optimization method                           NLMINB
   Number of model parameters                        13

   Number of observations                           220

Model Test User Model:

   Test statistic                                 7.918
   Degrees of freedom                                 8
   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.442

   Browne's residual (NT model-based) test
   Test statistic                                 8.054
   Degrees of freedom                                 8
   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.428

Parameter Estimates:

   Standard errors                             Standard
   Information                                 Expected
   Information saturated (h1) model          Structured

Latent Variables:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
   f1 =~
     fr       (L01)    0.690    0.059   11.657    0.000
     en       (L02)    0.671    0.060   11.273    0.000
     hi       (L03)    0.531    0.064    8.250    0.000
   f2 =~
     ar       (L04)    0.764    0.046   16.581    0.000
     al       (L05)    0.764    0.046   16.572    0.000
     ge       (L06)    0.616    0.053   11.601    0.000

Covariances:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
   f1 ~~
     f2                0.598    0.072    8.322    0.000

Variances:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)

     f1                1.000
     f2                1.000
    .fr                0.524
    .en                0.550
    .hi                0.718
    .ar                0.416
    .al                0.416
    .ge                0.620

Scaling Parameters:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
     fr                1.000    0.048   20.928    0.000
     en                1.000    0.048   20.928    0.000
     hi                1.000    0.048   20.928    0.000
     ar                1.000    0.048   20.928    0.000
     al                1.000    0.048   20.928    0.000
     ge                1.000    0.048   20.928    0.000

Defined Parameters:

                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)

resvar.fr <http://resvar.fr>         0.524    0.082    6.424    0.000
     resvar.en         0.550    0.080    6.880    0.000
     resvar.hi         0.718    0.068   10.496    0.000
     resvar.ar <http://resvar.ar>         0.416    0.070    5.907    0.000
     resvar.al <http://resvar.al>         0.416    0.070    5.913    0.000
     resvar.ge <http://resvar.ge>         0.620    0.065    9.478    0.000

lavaan NOTE:
    Standard errors and confidence intervals of the (nonlinear) defined
(:=)
    parameters are based on the first-order delta method; for strongly
    nonlinear definitions, se_def = "mc" (Monte Carlo) or se =
"bootstrap" may
    be more accurate.

I believe there may be an error in Table 4 of Cudeck's paper. Apart from
the double 'psi_2' label in the first column, the standard error for
psi_3 should be 0.068, not 0.080 (which is most likely a copy/paste error).

Yves.

The training combines methodological lectures with hands-on exercises in R using the LMest package, making it suitable for researchers, students, and industry professionals interested in analysing longitudinal data. Basic familiarity with R is helpful but not required.

Please feel free to share this announcement with interested colleagues.

Best regards,

Carlo

Carlo Pecoraro, Ph.D

messages.subject: Help understanding model fit measures
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm very new to SEM and lavaan, so apologies if this is a basic question, worded poorly  or I'm completely on the wrong track.

I'm fitting a structural equation model in lavaan using WLSMV because my behavioural outcome is binary. My sample is also not normally distributed. Sample size is 313.

The model ran successfully and produced the following fit indices:
CFI = .899 TLI = .911 RMSEA = .072 SRMR = .063

However, the scaled fit indices are much lower:
Scaled CFI = .342 Scaled TLI = .421

The output also shows a large difference between the standard and scaled baseline model chi-square statistics. I have read that although this does not support a good model fit, it should be interpreted along with other fit indices.

Model Test User Model:

                                              Standard      Scaled

  Test Statistic                               458.730     521.100

  Degrees of freedom                               174         174

  P-value (Unknown)                                 NA       0.000

  Scaling correction factor                                  1.143

  Shift parameter                                          119.804

    simple second-order correction

Model Test Baseline Model:

  Test statistic                              2965.033     680.456

  Degrees of freedom                               153         153

  P-value                                           NA       0.000

  Scaling correction factor                                  5.331

My confusion is that the RMSEA and SRMR appear to suggest at least acceptable fit, yet the scaled CFI/TLI imply extremely poor fit. I believe as my data is not normally distributed I should be paying attention to the scaled outputs. There is no robust CFI, TLI or RMSEA available.

Could someone help me understand:
Why can scaled CFI/TLI differ so dramatically from the standard values under WLSMV?
When the scaled and standard incremental fit indices tell such different stories, how would experienced SEM researchers typically interpret or report the model?

Any explanations or recommended references would be greatly appreciated. I'm still learning SEM and trying to understand what these indices are actually telling me.

Thanks in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

on behalf of local organizer Laura Trinchera, attached you will find the Call for Papers for the 2027 Meeting of the Structural Equation Modeling Working Group which will be held at NEOMA Business School from 17 to 19 March 2027 in Paris, France.

Keynote addresses will be held by Prof. Silvia Bianconcini (University of Bologna) and Prof. Fan Wallentin (Uppsala University). A Post-Conference Workshop will be held on 19 March, 2027 by Prof. Manuel Voelkle (University of Freiburg).

Abstracts can be submitted via the following online form: https://forms.gle/GeRUQsNnrkFKa72F7 until 15 December 2026.

For further information, please see the attached Call for Papers or visit the conference website: https://neoma-bs.com/faculty-and-research/research/2027-meeting-sem-working-group.

We look forward to your submissions!
Best regards,
Henrik Andersen

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
I've had some people ask me for the lavaan code for my book,
Understanding Structural Equation Models <https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.1201/9781003595267/understanding-structural-equation-models-phillip-wood>.

I have been working on a website for the book and have finished the lavaan markdown files for it. I'm still working on other software platforms, but felt that letting folks know about the lavaan code would be helpful. It's located here:
https://sites.google.com/view/understanding-structural-equa/home

Of course, if anyone has questions or comments about it, I'm more than happy to help out.
Phil Wood
philli...@gmail.com
